title: 1 Samuel 25:32–44
context: David blesses the LORD for sending Abigail and blesses her discretion for keeping him from bloodshed and from avenging himself. When Abigail tells Nabal what happened, his heart fails, and about ten days later the LORD strikes him so that he dies; David sees this as the LORD pleading his cause. David then takes Abigail as his wife, also marries Ahinoam of Jezreel, and the narrator adds that Saul had given Michal, David’s first wife, to Palti. Arminian and Reformed readers commonly read the section as shared ground about God’s vindication of those who leave vengeance to him (compare Romans 12:19). The account of David’s marriages is reported, not endorsed, and readers in both traditions commonly note that the law warned kings against multiplying wives (Deuteronomy 17:17).

verses.text: David said to Abigail, “Blessed is the LORD, the God of Israel, who sent you today to meet me!
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see David blessing the LORD for sending Abigail to meet him. He recognizes God’s hand in the intervention.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see David acknowledging God’s providence in sending a timely messenger. Readers in both traditions commonly see the verse as David’s heart turning back to God.

verses.text: Blessed is your discretion, and blessed are you, who have kept me today from blood guiltiness, and from avenging myself with my own hand.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see David blessing Abigail’s discretion for keeping him from bloodguilt and self-vengeance. He humbly accepts correction.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see David’s gratitude as a mark of a teachable heart. Both traditions commonly hold up this response as an example of receiving wise counsel well (compare Proverbs 12:16).

verses.text: For indeed, as the LORD the God of Israel lives, who has withheld me from harming you, unless you had hurried and come to meet me, surely there wouldn’t have been left to Nabal by the morning light so much as one who urinates on a wall.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see David admitting that he would have destroyed Nabal’s household if Abigail had not come. He is honest about how close he came to sin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see his confession as recognizing the LORD’s restraining hand. The expression again refers to every male, and both traditions commonly read the verse as a sober acknowledgment of what might have been.

verses.text: So David received from her hand that which she had brought him. Then he said to her, “Go up in peace to your house. Behold, I have listened to your voice and have granted your request.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see David receiving Abigail’s gift and sending her home in peace. He has listened to her voice and granted her request.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the peaceful resolution as the fruit of wise intercession and humble listening. Readers in both traditions commonly see the verse as the happy turning point of the story.

verses.text: Abigail came to Nabal; and behold, he held a feast in his house like the feast of a king. Nabal’s heart was merry within him, for he was very drunk. Therefore she told him nothing until the morning light.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Nabal feasting like a king and very drunk, unaware of the danger he caused. Abigail wisely waits until morning to speak.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the irony of Nabal acting like a king while insulting the true king-to-be. Both traditions commonly read the verse as continuing the portrait of his folly.

verses.text: In the morning, when the wine had gone out of Nabal, his wife told him these things; and his heart died within him, and he became as a stone.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Nabal’s heart dying within him when he hears what happened. The news of how near ruin came strikes him deeply.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see his collapse as the beginning of God’s judgment. Readers in both traditions commonly hold the exact medical nature of his condition with caution.

verses.text: About ten days later, the LORD struck Nabal, so that he died.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that about ten days later the LORD struck Nabal so that he died. Judgment comes from God, not from David’s sword.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s direct judgment as vindicating David’s restraint. Both traditions commonly read the verse as illustrating that vengeance belongs to the LORD (compare Deuteronomy 32:35).

verses.text: When David heard that Nabal was dead, he said, “Blessed is the LORD, who has pleaded the cause of my reproach from the hand of Nabal, and has kept back his servant from evil. The LORD has returned the evildoing of Nabal on his own head.” David sent and spoke concerning Abigail, to take her to himself as wife.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see David blessing the LORD for pleading his cause and keeping him from evil. He then sends for Abigail to become his wife.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see David recognizing that God has returned Nabal’s evil on his own head (compare Galatians 6:7). Readers in both traditions commonly read the proposal as reported narrative, without moral comment from the narrator.

verses.text: When David’s servants had come to Abigail to Carmel, they spoke to her, saying, “David has sent us to you, to take you to him as wife.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see David’s servants going to Carmel with his proposal. The request is made formally through messengers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the proposal as made formally and openly through David’s servants. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a factual report rather than a model.

verses.text: She arose and bowed herself with her face to the earth, and said, “Behold, your servant is a servant to wash the feet of the servants of my lord.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Abigail’s humble response, offering to wash the feet of David’s servants. Her humility remains consistent.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see her words as a customary expression of humility and willingness. Readers in both traditions commonly note that her character remains admirable throughout the story.

verses.text: Abigail hurriedly arose and rode on a donkey with her five maids who followed her; and she went after the messengers of David, and became his wife.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note Abigail rising quickly and going with her five maids to become David’s wife. She leaves her old household behind.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the account as reporting the marriage factually. Both traditions commonly note that Abigail is later named among David’s wives in Hebron (2 Samuel 3:3).

verses.text: David also took Ahinoam of Jezreel; and they both became his wives.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that David also took Ahinoam of Jezreel, so that both became his wives. The narrator records this without comment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the report of multiple wives as factual, not approving. Readers in both traditions commonly recall that the law warned kings against multiplying wives (Deuteronomy 17:17), and later chapters show the strains in David’s household.

verses.text: Now Saul had given Michal his daughter, David’s wife, to Palti the son of Laish, who was of Gallim.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note plainly that Saul had given Michal, David’s wife, to Palti the son of Laish. Saul’s action treats his daughter as a political tool.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as preparing for later events, when Michal is taken back from her husband Paltiel (2 Samuel 3:14–16). Both traditions commonly read it as a factual note that reveals the brokenness of the royal household.
